email.scenario: As part of the regional citizen science program's backyard habitat monitoring project, you were mailed a rain gauge to track weekly precipitation. When you unpacked it, you noticed the printed markings use a different measurement scale than the program's instructions describe, so every reading you take is impossible to log accurately.
email.subject: Incorrect Scale on Mailed Rain Gauge
bullets: Explain that the rain gauge you received has markings printed in the wrong measurement scale.
Request either a replacement gauge or a chart for converting your current readings.
Ask whether the readings you have already logged need to be corrected.

academicDiscussion.professorPost: Many regional archives are moving away from digitizing their collections in chronological order. Instead, staff now prioritize whichever records outside researchers request most often, since that keeps popular materials available quickly. Archivists have limited time each week, so favoring frequent requests can leave entire decades of records untouched for years. Which approach should archives follow, and why?

studentPosts.name: Maya
studentPosts.post: I think request-driven digitization makes sense. Archivists have only a few hours a week for this work, so scanning whatever researchers actually need first means that effort isn't wasted on records nobody is currently using. A chronological plan sounds fair, but it could leave popular, historically significant collections locked away for years while staff work through less-requested decades.

studentPosts.name: Devon
studentPosts.post: I disagree with Maya. If archives only chase current demand, entire decades could stay undigitized indefinitely, especially periods nobody has discovered yet. Chronological digitization guarantees the whole collection eventually becomes accessible, so future researchers aren't blocked by today's popularity. Staffing limits are real, but that's an argument for more funding, not for permanently skipping unrequested records.
